The package got smaller: compare the unit price and the cash needed for whole packs

Use four graphics to compare package prices, recurring checkout cash and the cost of product consumed versus stock still in the cupboard.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two hypothetical packages of the same usable product

Interactive planning lab

Comparison minus reference price per kilogram15.38%
Comparison minus reference checkout cash in month 1$12
Difference in total checkout cash over the selected months$90

Original hypothetical comparison in nominal CAD of the same usable product, quality and monthly quantity. All package prices and sizes are assumptions, not live offers or survey observations. Both alternatives start with no stock. At each month’s start, buy the fewest whole packages needed to cover that month’s consumption after using stock carried forward. Any unused quantity remains usable for the next month without spoilage, loss or storage cost. Prices and package sizes stay constant throughout the selected horizon. The purchase cost assigned to unused stock reconciles prior cash paid; it is not cash in the bank, a resale quote or a guaranteed recoverable value. No sales tax, coupons, delivery fees, interest, membership cost, nutrition comparison or change in consumption is calculated. A unit-price comparison should use the same measurement unit and genuinely comparable contents.

The central idea

The sticker price, price per kilogram and cash paid at checkout measure different things. Compare the same quantity, then carry leftover stock into the next purchase.

01

Put both packages on the same measurement basis

A package can keep the same shelf price while containing less product. The total price alone would show no increase, but the price of the quantity you actually use has changed. For a household budget, that difference matters when you keep buying the same amount of the product over time.

The Office of Consumer Affairs’ unit-pricing guide explains how a standard weight, volume or item measure helps compare similar products. It also describes shrinkflation as a reduction in quantity without a matching reduction in the retail price. This tool uses invented package examples rather than naming a brand or quoting a current offer.

Compare contents that serve the same purpose and use the same unit. A kilogram of one product is not automatically equivalent to a kilogram of another if concentration, quality or usable yield differs. The model assumes comparable usable contents so it can isolate the quantity and cash arithmetic.

02

A percentage weight reduction and a percentage unit-price increase differ

The default reference package costs CAD 6 for 750 grams. Its unit price is CAD 8 per kilogram. The comparison package costs the same CAD 6 for 650 grams, or about CAD 9.23 per kilogram.

The package contains 100 grams less, a reduction of about 13.33% from the original 750 grams. The unit price rises by about 15.38%, calculated as (6 ÷ 650) ÷ (6 ÷ 750) − 1. The two percentages differ because their denominators differ.

The bar chart uses price per kilogram for both packages. Change the comparison price independently of its size to see whether a lower sticker price compensates for the smaller contents. The tool can show a saving as well as an increase; its labels do not assume the comparison package is always more expensive.

03

Budget for the whole packages you can actually buy

The default household consumes 6,000 grams each month and starts with no stock. In month 1, eight reference packages supply exactly that amount and cost CAD 48. The comparison needs ten whole packages, costing CAD 60 and supplying 6,500 grams.

Only 6,000 of those grams are consumed in the month. The remaining 500 grams are carried forward. In month 2, that stock reduces the quantity that must be bought, so the model does not round the full 6,000 grams upward again as though the cupboard were empty.

Buying fractional packages would produce a smooth consumption-cost estimate, but it would not describe the checkout payment. Conversely, rounding every month independently and discarding the leftover stock would overstate future purchases under this model’s no-waste assumption.

04

Keep unused stock separate from money available to spend

Across twelve default months, the reference alternative buys 96 packages for CAD 576. The comparison buys 111 packages for CAD 666 and ends with 150 grams unused. The cumulative checkout difference is CAD 90.

At the comparison unit cost, the 72,000 grams consumed have a purchase cost of about CAD 664.62. The remaining stock has an allocated purchase cost of about CAD 1.38. Together they reconcile the CAD 666 already paid. The stock allocation is not another charge and is not money that remains in the bank.

The stacked bars make that distinction visible for both alternatives. Their totals compare actual modeled checkout cash, while the segments explain how much of the purchased quantity was consumed or still held. Different ending inventories mean the cash difference is not exactly the same as the cost difference for equal quantities consumed.

05

Test package size and price without assuming a bulk bargain

The matrix replaces the comparison package size and price while holding monthly use, the reference package and the selected horizon constant. Every cell applies the same whole-package rule and carries stock forward. A larger package need not have a lower unit price, and even a low unit price can require a larger payment on the first shopping trip.

Read a positive cell as more total checkout cash than the reference and a negative cell as less. These are selected price-and-size scenarios, not observed supermarket prices or forecasts. They also assume that every gram remains usable.

For a real comparison, separately consider storage space, spoilage, the risk of buying more than the household will use and any extra shopping or delivery cost. This model holds those items at zero; it does not turn a favourable unit price into a recommendation to buy more.

06

Connect the unit calculation to the recurring cash budget

Record the price, net quantity and common unit when comparing two offers. Estimate the quantity the household actually uses, then check how many whole packs are required for the next purchase after counting usable stock already at home.

The cash chart follows cumulative payments, so it can reveal a larger early shopping payment even when the long-run unit cost looks attractive. It does not calculate a bank balance or assume that borrowing fills a shortfall. Fit the payment into the broader food and household budget.

Finally, revise the assumptions when the price, package size or usage changes. A unit-price calculation explains the cost of quantity, while a purchase calendar explains how that cost reaches the household’s cash account.
